mcqs.question: What's the actual maintenance problem with the instanceof chain in totalArea?
options: Adding a new shape type requires editing every call site that has its own copy of this chain, or it silently contributes nothing
It runs slower than a for-each loop over an array
It can't compile because Java forbids chained else-if with instanceof
It only works for exactly three shape types, never more or fewer
mcqs.explanation: Every duplicated instanceof chain needs its own edit when a new type is added, or it quietly ignores that type. It compiles fine, isn't inherently slow for small lists, and works for any number of branches you're willing to add.

mcqs.question: Per the diagram, what does adding a Pentagon type cost in the polymorphic version vs the if/else version?
options: The same cost in both — one new class either way
Nothing in either version, since both are automatically extensible
One new class with zero edits to existing call sites, versus an edit at every call site that has its own type-check chain
More cost in the polymorphic version, since every subclass needs its own vtable
mcqs.explanation: The polymorphic version only needs a new Pentagon class; the if/else version needs a new branch wherever the type check is duplicated. The costs are not equal, and per-subclass vtable entries aren't a meaningful added cost for the developer.

mcqs.question: What's the actual runtime cost polymorphism adds compared to a direct, compile-time-resolved call?
options: A full linear scan through every possible subtype at each call
A vtable lookup — one extra indirection, often eliminated by JIT inline caching in hot loops
A network round-trip to resolve the correct implementation
No cost at all — dispatch is always free regardless of mechanism
mcqs.explanation: Dynamic dispatch costs one indirection through a vtable, which JIT compilers frequently optimize away via inline caching when the type at a call site is predictable. There's no linear scan and certainly no network involved, and the cost isn't literally zero.

mcqs.question: Why is "polymorphism removes the need for conditionals entirely" wrong?
options: Because well-designed code never uses if statements, period
Because forcing every conditional into a class hierarchy always improves performance
Because interfaces cannot contain any conditional logic internally
Polymorphism only replaces conditionals that dispatch on type; conditionals like range validation or business rules aren't about type at all and shouldn't be forced into a class hierarchy
mcqs.explanation: The target is type-switch conditionals specifically, not conditionals in general — forcing an unrelated validation check into a class hierarchy usually makes code worse. Performance isn't the point, and interfaces can absolutely contain conditional logic in their default or implementing methods.
